title: Improving minigrep, and zero-cost iterators
summary: Removing clone from Config::build by taking an iterator, rewriting search with filter and collect, choosing between loops and iterators, and why iterator chains compile to the same machine code as hand-written loops.

blocks.md: Chapter 12's `Config::build` cloned two strings because it received a **slice** of arguments it did not own. But `env::args()` already gives an iterator of owned `String`s. Pass that iterator in, and `build` can take ownership of the values instead of copying them.

blocks.explain: `impl Iterator<Item = String>` accepts any iterator of strings: `env::args()` in `main`, or a vector's `into_iter()` in a test. `args` is `mut` because `next` advances it. The error messages are also more specific now.

blocks.title: search with adapters
blocks.md:
The loop version of `search` built a vector by hand. With adapters it says what it means:

```rust
pub fn search<'a>(query: &str, contents: &'a str) -> Vec<&'a str> {
    contents
        .lines()
        .filter(|line| line.contains(query))
        .collect()
}
```

There is no mutable `results` vector left. Without shared mutable state, a future change could even run the filtering in parallel. Going further, `search` could return `impl Iterator<Item = &'a str>` and let the caller decide whether to collect at all.

blocks.title: Loops or iterators?
blocks.md: Most Rust programmers prefer the iterator style once they are used to it: it states the goal (`filter` the lines that contain the query) instead of the mechanics (index, push, increment). Loops remain the right choice when the body has complex control flow, early returns with side effects, or several outputs at once. Both compile to fast code, as the next section shows.

blocks.title: Zero-cost abstractions
blocks.md:
*The Rust Programming Language* benchmarks a search over the full text of *The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes*: the `for` loop version and the iterator version take essentially the **same time**. *Programming Rust* explains why: after monomorphization and inlining, the chain of `Map`, `Filter` and `Range` structs disappears and what remains is the loop you would have written. Bjarne Stroustrup's definition of **zero-overhead**: what you do not use, you do not pay for; what you do use, you could not hand-code any better.

The book's audio decoder example shows how far this goes. This chain computes a linear prediction over 12 coefficients:

```rust
let prediction = coefficients.iter()
    .zip(&buffer[i - 12..i])
    .map(|(&c, &s)| c * s as i64)
    .sum::<i64>() >> qlp_shift;
```

The compiler knows there are exactly 12 iterations and **unrolls** the loop into 12 multiply-adds with no loop counter, no bounds checks and the coefficients kept in registers.

blocks.title: Config::build from an iterator
blocks.md: Finish `Config::build` so it reads from an iterator instead of indexing a slice, with no `clone`. `main` passes each simulated argument list with `into_iter()`, the same way `env::args()` would.

questions.q: Why could the new `Config::build` drop the `clone` calls?
options: It takes an iterator of owned Strings and moves them into Config
questions.explanation: Owning the iterator means owning its items.

options: Calling next advances the iterator, which mutates it

questions.q: Compared with the loop version, the iterator version of search is...
Iterator chains are compiled by inlining and optimization into code close to a hand-written loop.
questions.explanation: Sometimes even unrolled, as in the audio decoder.

points: Taking `impl Iterator<Item = String>` lets `Config::build` own its arguments without cloning.
Prefer iterators for clarity; keep loops for complex control flow.
Iterators are zero-cost: they compile to code as fast as hand-written loops.

terms.def: A high-level feature that compiles to code as efficient as what you would write by hand.
An optimization that replaces a loop with repeated copies of its body, removing the loop counter.
